title: Breton Numbers
bodyHtml:
Breton is a language spoken by approximately 200,000 people in Brittany, France. Part of the Celtic family of the Indo-European languages, it is distantly related to English, as well as other European languages such as French and Russian.

Below are some equations in Breton:

trizek + daouzek=pemp warn ugent
unan ha pevar-ugent ÷ nav=nav
pevar ha tri-ugent – ugent=pevar ha daou-ugent
seizh warn ugent + pevarzek=unan ha daou-ugent
daou × seizh=pevarzek
kant ÷ daou=hanter kant
nav × c’hwec’h=pevar ha hanter kant
c’hwec’h ha tri-ugent ÷ tri=daou warn ugent
c’hwezek × c’hwec’h=c’hwezek ha pevar-ugent
daouzek × pemp=tri-ugent

E1. In the Answer Sheets, fill in the gaps in the following equations.

  1. pevar-ugent ÷ pemp =
  2. pemp ha hanter kant – daouzek =
  3. nav warn ugent + = tri ha daou-ugent
  4. kant ÷ = pemp

E2. As well as an interesting numbering system, Breton has an unusual method of forming the plurals of some nouns, which is partly connected to the numbering system. Here are three plural nouns in Breton: which of them means “(one person’s) eyes”? Record your answer in the Answer Sheets.

(a) elerc’h     (b) daoulagad     (c) perennoù

E3. An “irregular” number in the Breton system is triwec’h. It represents a number between 10 and 20. Which one? Record your answer in the Answer Sheets.

questions.promptHtml: Which number between 10 and 20 does triwec’h represent? Give a figure.
questions.partPrompt: The "irregular" Breton number triwec'h represents a number between 10 and 20. Which one?

hints.text: Start with the shortest lines, the ones where a multiplication or a division has simple one-word inputs, such as the lines built from daou, seizh, kant and nav. Those pin down the basic digit words before you worry about the long compound expressions.

Breton does not count in tens: its base is twenty. One word means 20, and larger round numbers are built from it, so a prefix like tri- or pevar- attached to that word gives 60 and 80. The little word ha means "and" (addition), warn signals "plus twenty", and hanter means "half", so hanter kant is half of a hundred.

Try the line kant divided by daou = hanter kant. If daou is 2, then hanter kant is half of kant, which fits hanter meaning "half". Now test the line nav times c'hwec'h = pevar ha hanter kant: 9 times 6 is 54, and 54 is 4 plus 50, so ha really does join an extra unit onto a round number.

explanationHtml:
Turning the equations into arithmetic

Each line is a genuine sum, so the trick is to find one line with few unknowns and use it as an anchor. Look at line 2: unan ha pevar-ugent divided by nav equals nav. If a number divided by nav gives nav back, that number must be nav squared. The only squares that a short Breton phrase like this is likely to hide are 81 (9 times 9) or 100 (10 times 10) or 64 (8 times 8). Line 6, kant divided by daou = hanter kant, shows that kant is a round number and hanter means "half" ("half a hundred"). So kant is 100, daou is 2, and hanter kant is 50. Then in line 7, nav times c'hwec'h equals pevar ha hanter kant, that is something plus 50. Nine times six is 54, which is 4 plus 50: so nav is 9, c'hwec'h is 6, pevar is 4, and ha means "plus".

Back to line 2: nav squared is 81, and 81 is 1 plus 80. So unan is 1 and pevar-ugent is 80.

A base-twenty (vigesimal) system

Because pevar is 4 and pevar-ugent is 80, the element ugent must be 20: "four twenties". That is what linguists call a vigesimal system, counting in twenties rather than tens. French does something similar with quatre-vingts "four twenties" for 80.

Line 10 confirms it: daouzek times pemp = tri-ugent. If tri is 3, then tri-ugent is 60, and 60 is 12 times 5, so daouzek is 12 and pemp is 5. Line 5, daou times seizh = pevarzek, gives 2 times 7 equals 14, so seizh is 7 and pevarzek is 14.

The word warn

Line 1 says trizek plus daouzek equals pemp warn ugent. Since pemp is 5 and the whole thing is 13 plus 12 = 25, warn ugent must add 20: "five on twenty". Line 8 checks out too: (6 plus 60) divided by 3 is 22, written daou warn ugent, "two on twenty". So numbers from 21 to 29 use warn ugent, while multiples of twenty plus a remainder use ha: unan ha daou-ugent is 1 plus 40 = 41, which matches line 4 (27 plus 14).

The teens

Notice a pattern: daouzek 12, trizek 13, pevarzek 14. The digit word plus the ending -zek gives 10 plus that digit. So 16 is built from c'hwec'h in the same way, and line 9 shows the word: c'hwezek times c'hwec'h = c'hwezek ha pevar-ugent, i.e. 16 times 6 = 96 = 16 plus 80. Consistent.

Solving E1

  • a. 80 divided by 5 is 16 — the teen word built on "six".
  • b. pemp ha hanter kant is 5 plus 50 = 55; 55 minus 12 is 43, which is 3 plus 40, so it is expressed as "three and two-twenties".
  • c. nav warn ugent is 9 plus 20 = 29; the answer 43 minus 29 is 14, a teen word already seen in the data.
  • d. 100 divided by what gives 5? Twenty — the base word of the whole system.

E2: eyes come in pairs

Some languages have special "dual" plurals for things that naturally come in twos: eyes, ears, hands. The Breton plural for "eyes" is built with the number 2, daou, at the front, which is exactly the connection to the numeral system the problem hints at. Of the three candidates, only daoulagad begins with daou-, so that is the one. (elerc'h is "swans" and perennoù is "pears".)

E3: triwec'h

The regular teens use -zek on a digit. triwec'h instead looks like tri "three" fused with c'hwec'h "six" — not "three plus six" but "three sixes", 3 times 6 = 18. Multiplying inside a numeral is natural in a language that already says "four twenties" for 80, and it explains why the number is called irregular: it is the odd one out among the teens.

Note the solution page is headed "Breton Numerals" while the problem page is headed "Breton Numbers" — the problem title used here follows the problem page. Point split across the six blanks (2/2/2/2/3/4 = 15) is my own; the booklet gives no per-part breakdown. Apostrophes in Breton data are transcribed as the curly right single quote as printed; ASCII-apostrophe variants accepted where relevant.
